storyNotes.originalText: Jacob stopped at a WELL. He met Rachel, the daughter of his uncle Laban.
storyNotes.cleanText: Jacob stopped at a well. He met Rachel, the daughter of his uncle Laban.

storyNotes.originalText: Laban brought Jacob to his HOME. Jacob stayed with him for a month.
storyNotes.cleanText: Laban brought Jacob to his home. Jacob stayed with him for a month.

storyNotes.originalText: Laban agreed to let Jacob MARRY his daughter Rachel in exchange for seven years of work.
storyNotes.cleanText: Laban agreed to let Jacob marry his daughter Rachel in exchange for seven years of work.

storyNotes.originalText: Jacob worked for Laban for seven years. Because he LOVED Rachel, it seemed like just a few days.
storyNotes.cleanText: Jacob worked for Laban for seven years. Because he loved Rachel, it seemed like just a few days.

storyNotes.originalText: After his wedding feast, Jacob realized he’d been TRICKED into marrying Rachel’s sister Leah.
storyNotes.cleanText: After his wedding feast, Jacob realized he’d been tricked into marrying Rachel’s sister Leah.

storyNotes.originalText: Laban said, “You can marry Rachel, too. But you must also WORK for me for seven more years.”
storyNotes.cleanText: Laban said, “You can marry Rachel, too. But you must also work for me for seven more years.”

storyNotes.originalText: Jacob married Rachel and loved her MORE than Leah. He worked for Laban for seven more years.
storyNotes.cleanText: Jacob married Rachel and loved her more than Leah. He worked for Laban for seven more years.

questions.question: Have you ever been tricked or pranked?
questions.notes: Open or rhetorical prompt; no parenthetical answer supplied in this source.

questions.question: Or have you ever tricked or pranked someone?
questions.answer: Allow a few children to respond.

questions.question: What day is it?
What unkind trick did Jacob play and why did he do it?
questions.answer: He pretended to be Esau to fool his father so he could steal his brother’s blessing.

questions.question: Because Esau was so angry, what did Jacob have to do?
questions.answer: Run away to live with his uncle.

questions.question: Whose house was he trying to find?
What was Laban’s daughter’s name?
What two things did Jacob do to show how happy he was?
questions.answer: He kissed Rachel and started crying.

questions.question: What did Laban do when he met Jacob?
What do you think Jacob told his uncle about?
questions.answer: Running away from Esau; his dream where God made promises to him.

questions.question: How long did Jacob stay with Laban after arriving in town?
But what did Jacob say to Laban?
questions.answer: I'll work for you for seven years if I can marry your daughter, Rachel.

questions.question: How many years did he offer to work?
What was the name of Rachel's older sister?
What did Jacob say?
questions.answer: I'll work for seven years if I can marry Rachel.

questions.question: How many days do you think that is?
questions.answer: Have the kids shout out various guesses.

questions.question: Why?
questions.answer: Because he loved Rachel so much.

questions.question: Who did he want to marry?
Who was it?
How did Jacob not notice?
questions.notes: Open or rhetorical prompt; no parenthetical answer supplied in this source.

questions.question: What was Laban’s answer?
questions.answer: It's our tradition to give away the older daughter to be married first.

questions.question: If he married Rachel, how many wives would he have?
How many wives does the Bible tell us we're supposed to have?
What did Jacob decide to do?
What does the Bible say about Jacob's love for Rachel and Leah?
How do you think Leah felt knowing Jacob loved Rachel more?
So how does the story of Jacob, Leah, and Rachel teach us, strengthen us, encourage us, or give us hope?
questions.notes: Open or rhetorical prompt; no parenthetical answer supplied in this source.

questions.question: How did Jacob's sinful trick hurt the people involved?
questions.answer: Esau was angry, Isaac felt hurt, Jacob had to run away from his family.

questions.question: How did Laban's sinful trick hurt the people involved?
questions.answer: Jacob's family became a jealous mess; Leah and Rachel fought, etc.

questions.question: When God sees the evil and sinful things people do, how does he feel?
To pay the price to rescue us from our sins, what did Jesus do?
To show he was done paying for our sins, what happened to God's Son Jesus on the third day?
And though we've all sinned like Jacob and Laban, though we’ve hurt others and angered God, what does God promise to do if we believe the good news of Jesus?
questions.answer: Give us forever life in his good kingdom.

questions.question: What is he teaching us here?
questions.answer: To think about what we’d want done to us and do that to others.

questions.question: Would they want someone to trick them?
questions.notes: Open or rhetorical prompt; no parenthetical answer supplied in this source.

questions.question: What did Jacob learn from talking to the shepherds at the well?
questions.answer: He was near his Uncle Laban’s house

questions.question: Who came walking to the well while Jacob was talking?
How long did Jacob live with his uncle?
When Laban said, “You shouldn’t work for free,” what did Jacob say?
questions.answer: I’ll work seven years if I can marry Rachel

questions.question: How did those seven years feel to Jacob? Why?
questions.answer: Like a few days because he loved her

questions.question: How did Laban trick Jacob?
questions.answer: He secretly gave his daughter Leah to be Jacob’s wife

questions.question: When Jacob asked, “Why did you trick me?”, what did Laban say?
questions.answer: It’s our custom for the older daughter to be married first

questions.question: After he married Leah, what deal did Jacob and Laban make?
questions.answer: Wait one week, marry Rachel, work for seven more years

questions.question: How did Jacob feel about his wives?
What is a marriage supposed to be?

reviewFlags.text: The original source quotes Matthew 7:12a in ESV with a trailing ellipsis. Verse activities retain this exact source text; the teacher must select and verify the final BSB excerpt, then synchronize all seven verse-linked fields in Review Studio.

The Review Activity introduction on source page 10 says “eight story notes,” while the 14-page ODT actually contains seven STORY NOTE boxes (WELL, HOME, MARRY, LOVED, TRICKED, WORK, MORE). Only the seven documented notes were converted; confirm whether a card/resource was omitted.
Review the 10 Multiple Choice adaptations and all 20 authored incorrect answer choices; 45 original questions are preserved separately.
Review authored false facts and selected Sort, True/False, and Maze facts. Prepared fact IDs are distinct and exactly match canonical statements and truth values.
Review unrelated vocabulary decoys for Odd Words and Checkboxes. Their suggested origin is explicit.
Review the five newly written Circle the Mistakes errors and corresponding corrections, along with the adapted Finish the Story, Story Order, and drawing captions.

The source discusses arranged marriage customs, a deceptive marriage substitution, Jacob having two wives, jealousy, gender and marriage teachings, sin, God’s anger, and salvation through Jesus. Teacher should review age appropriateness and theological fidelity; do not treat authored questions as doctrinal judgments.
Both original Important Ideas must remain unchanged (“sin hurts others.” and “Sin angers God. That's why we need Jesus.”). Review Big Idea selection and the new Pixel Picture phrase.
Verify real crossword interlocking, both word-search layouts, letter/pixel engines, SVG/PDF print fit, and all three numbered presets; local content checks alone do not prove printable success.
Official current candidate-specific repo schema/semantic validation, Review Studio 27-module preflight, and teacher BSB rights verification have NOT RUN / are pending. No approval is claimed.

Only the 14-page ODT source was supplied; no standalone slideshow, Sheep Pens, Story Note Picture cards, Heart Weaves, or other referenced resource sheets were supplied. No missing material was invented.
